intro: Family is one of the first things people talk about. This lesson gives you the words for your close family, your wider family and your family by marriage, and the sentences to present them.
objectifs: Name the people in your close and wider family (parents, brothers and sisters, uncles, cousins…).
Use words for family by marriage and new families (in-laws, stepfather, half-sister).
Present your family with “have got”, the possessive ’s and possessive adjectives.
Avoid common traps: “parents” vs “relatives”, and irregular plurals (children).

texte: Many words come in male / female pairs. At home, people often say “mum” and “dad” (American English: “mom” and “dad”).
“Child” has an irregular plural: “children”. “Siblings” (brothers and sisters) is a little formal; in conversation, people usually say “brothers and sisters”.
exemples: My mum is a teacher and my dad is a taxi driver.
They have two children: a son and a daughter.
sections.note: “Wife” means a married woman (someone's partner). For any female adult, say “a woman”.

texte: Add “grand-” for the generation of your grandparents and your grandchildren: grandmother (grandma, granny), grandfather (grandpa), grandson, granddaughter.
“Cousin” is the same word for a man and a woman. For the generation before your grandparents, add “great-”: great-grandmother.
exemples: My grandparents live in a village near Bafoussam.

sections.titre: Family by marriage and new families
texte: For your husband's or wife's family, add “-in-law”: mother-in-law, brother-in-law. In the plural, the first word takes the s: sisters-in-law. All of them together: “my in-laws”.

In a new family, “step-” is for your parent's new partner or their children: stepfather (your mother's husband, not your father), stepsister. “Half-” is for a brother or sister with only one parent the same as you: half-brother.
Careful: “mother-in-law” is your partner's mother; “stepmother” is your father's wife. They are two different people.
exemples: My mother-in-law makes the best ndolé.
Leo is my half-brother: we have the same dad.

texte: In English, “parents” means only your mother and father. For other people in your family (uncles, cousins…), say “relatives” or “relations”.
“Family” is a singular noun: “My family is big.” In British English you also hear “My family are all tall” when you think of the people one by one.
exemples: We have relatives in France and Belgium.

texte: To say how many brothers, sisters or children you have, use “have got” (lesson 5) or “have”: “I've got two sisters.” / “I have two sisters.” The question: “Have you got any brothers or sisters?” or “Do you have any brothers or sisters?”.
For family links, use the possessive ’s (lesson 15): “my sister's husband”, “my parents' house”.
Useful phrases: “I'm an only child” (no brothers or sisters), “He's my older brother”, “She's my younger sister”, “We're twins”, “I'm married / single / divorced”.
exemples: Have you got any brothers or sisters? — Yes, I've got one brother.
Question and answer with have got.
No, I haven't. I'm an only child.
My sister's husband is a nurse.

formule: I've got + number + family word · my sister's husband · my parents' house
prononciation: “mother”, “brother”, “other”: the o is /ʌ/ (like in “but”) and the th is /ð/: /ˈmʌðə/, /ˈbrʌðə/.
“daughter” /ˈdɔːtə/: you don't say the gh. The same in “granddaughter” /ˈɡrændɔːtə/.
“aunt” is /ɑːnt/ in British English and /ænt/ in American English (like “ant”, the insect).
“niece” /niːs/ rhymes with “piece”; “nephew” /ˈnefjuː/ has the stress on the first syllable.
erreurs: My parents are all at the wedding: my uncles, my cousins…
My relatives are all at the wedding.
“Parents” = mother and father only; the wider family = relatives.
“Cousin” is the same for male and female.
Use the possessive ’s for family links.
How many brothers do you have got?
How many brothers have you got? / How many brothers do you have?
After a plural in -s, add only the apostrophe.

dialogue.contexte: In Brussels, Inès shows family photos to her colleague Kofi.
lignes: Yes! These are my parents, and this is my younger brother, Sami.
And who's the woman with the baby?
That's my aunt, my mum's sister. The baby is her granddaughter.
So the baby is your cousin's daughter?
Exactly. Have you got a big family?
Very big! I've got four sisters and about thirty cousins in Ghana.
Thirty cousins! I'm jealous. I've only got two.

mots: a child with no brothers or sisters
having a husband or a wife
not married, not in a relationship
one of two children born at the same time to the same mother
the child of your son or daughter
We visit my in-laws every Sunday.
the family of your husband or wife
the child of your aunt or uncle

exercices.consigne: Complete with the right family word.
Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: We have parents in Douala: two uncles and a cousin.
My mother-in-law is my father's new wife.
My stepmother is my father's new wife.
Do you have got any brothers or sisters?
Have you got any brothers or sisters? / Do you have any brothers or sisters?

exercices.consigne: Present your family in four or five sentences: your parents, your brothers and sisters, your wider family.
items: I've got a small family. My parents live in Liège. I've got one older sister, Clara. Her husband is from Canada and they've got two children, so I've got a nephew and a niece. My grandparents live in a village near Namur.

a_retenir: parents = mother and father only; the wider family = relatives.
child → children; wife → wives; cousin is male and female.
-in-law for family by marriage (mother-in-law), step- for a new family (stepfather), half- for a half-brother.
Family links with ’s: my sister's husband, my parents' house.
I've got two brothers. / I'm an only child. / Have you got any brothers or sisters?
